title: Until 2019, the kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder near Paris
body: From 1889 to 2019 the kilogram was defined by one object: a golf-ball-sized cylinder of 90% platinum and 10% iridium, kept under nested bell jars in a vault outside Paris that takes three separate keys to open. Copies went to countries around the world and came back for comparison only three times, in 1889, 1948 and 1989. Those checks revealed a problem: the prototype and its copies were drifting apart, by roughly **50 micrograms over a century**, and nobody could say which was right. On 20 May 2019 the kilogram was redefined through a fixed value of the Planck constant, which can’t drift or be scratched.

slides.label: by which the prototype seems to have drifted from its copies in a century
slides.text: A tiny amount, but with the kilogram tied to one object there was no way to tell which cylinder had changed.

slides.heading: Le Grand K
items: 90% platinum, 10% iridium, about 39 mm tall and wide
Kept under nested bell jars in a basement vault at the BIPM in Saint-Cloud
Three keys, held separately, to open the vault
Compared with its copies only in 1889, 1948 and 1989

slides.heading: Why a constant
slides.text: The metre was already defined by the speed of light. On 16 November 2018 the General Conference on Weights and Measures voted to treat mass the same way: fix the Planck constant at exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, and a Kibble balance can realise a kilogram anywhere, with no master object to guard.

slides.heading: Earliest first
items: Copies compared for the last time
slides.explanation: 1875, 1889, 1989 and 20 May 2019. The last comparison of the copies is what revealed the drift.
